Krakatoa. Located in the Sunda Strait between Java and Sumatra in Indonesia, this island sits along the subduction zone where the Indo-Australian Plate slides beneath the Eurasian Plate. Krakatoa is famous for its cataclysmic eruption in August 1883, which released energy equivalent to 200 megatons of TNT and destroyed over seventy percent of the island and its surrounding archipelago. The explosion generated the loudest sound in recorded history, which was heard three thousand miles away on Rodrigues Island in the Indian Ocean and ruptured the eardrums of sailors forty miles away. The eruption triggered devastating tsunamis up to one hundred twenty feet high that swept across the coasts of Java and Sumatra, destroying hundreds of villages and causing over 36,000 casualties. The disaster was among the first historical events spread instantaneously around the globe via the newly completed worldwide submarine telegraph network, pioneering global telecommunications tracking. The eruption also produced global atmospheric phenomena, injecting aerosols into the stratosphere that caused temperatures to drop worldwide and generated vivid red sunsets, which reportedly inspired Edvard Munch's painting The Scream. From the collapsed caldera, a new volcanic cone emerged in 1927, Anak Krakatau, which means Child of Krakatoa, and continues to grow at a rapid rate. In 2018, a major collapse of Anak Krakatau triggered a landslide-induced tsunami in the Sunda Strait that killed over 400 people. Krakatoa stands as a peer to the stratovolcano Vesuvius, and resembles Mount Tambora, a nearby Indonesian volcano whose 1815 eruption was even larger, and shares global cooling effects with Mount Pinatubo, another Philippine volcano that caused notable cooling in 1991.
